skills: Year 1
The vocabulary of the field - hazard, vulnerability, resilience, risk - used precisely (DMG 101, DMG 102, DMG 103).
A map you drew yourself, with a legend, scale and north point (DMG 111 Cartography and Mapping Techniques).
Statistics and a spreadsheet from STAT 101 and CSE 101 carried into every lab after them.
The DMES student tutors for 100-level courses used in week two, not week twelve.
Year 2
Surveying and GIS as working tools, not demonstrations (DMG 112, DMG 211) - one real map per lab.
Planning theory applied to a place you know (DMG 104, DMG 204).
The stream decided on paper (tool 1): Humanitarian, Climate, or Environmental Risk Reduction Technology - and the first stream courses taken.
A reading habit in Bangladesh's own disaster record: one event studied properly each month (tool 3).
Year 3
Qualitative and quantitative research methods done on your own data (DMG 370, DMG 371).
Fieldwork logged the way DMG 384 teaches it: hazards identified from observation, needs assessed, people treated with respect.
A stream specialism visible in your electives and lab choices (DMG 381-385, 471).
An organisation shortlisted for DMG 497 - NGO, government, media house or research centre - and a conversation held.
Year 4
DMG 497: three months inside an organisation, a portfolio, an 8,000-12,000-word report and a recommendation letter.

The final requirement chosen and done: DMG 499 dissertation (15,000-20,000 words, defended), DMG 498 capstone (field study, 8,000-12,000 words, presented) or DMG 496 study abroad (6 credits, approved).
DMG 401 Bangladesh policy and practice read against what you saw in the field.
A CV that names the methods you can run - survey, interview, GIS, remote sensing, hazard analysis - with one example each.
dept.career_intro: The programme page says internships with NGOs, government organisations and media houses expose students to the field, and that the degree makes students eligible for higher study. The directions below are the common ones for a disaster-management graduate; none is a BRACU rule, and the department prints no placement list of its own.
careers: Humanitarian response and NGOs
Programme, protection, shelter and camp work with national and international organisations.
Option A courses (DMG 221-224, 321-326, 422), DMG 497 in a humanitarian organisation, the Response Team (BURT).
Government and local government
Disaster management offices, planning bodies, climate and environment agencies, recruited through examinations and projects.
DMG 401 policy and practice, DMG 104/204 planning, GIS (DMG 211, 411); the general sections those examinations carry.
Climate adaptation and research
Climate projects, adaptation planning, negotiation support, research institutes.
Option B courses (DMG 241-245, 341-346, 441, 442), DMG 452, a DMG 499 dissertation with real data.
Risk modelling, GIS and remote sensing
Hazard mapping, risk-sensitive land-use planning, early-warning systems.
Option C courses (DMG 247, 345, 347), DMG 381 Remote Sensing, DMG 411, DMG 385; a portfolio of maps.
Environmental assessment and consultancy
Impact assessments, pollution analysis, compliance for projects and firms.
DMG 242 Environmental Impact Assessment, DMG 251, DMG 342, DMG 344.
Urban planning and shelter design
Settlement planning, shelter and site planning after disasters, urban risk.
DMG 331/332/431 Shelter Design and Site Planning (Option A labs), DMG 303 Urban Design, DMG 411.
Security, safety and resilience
Corporate and public safety, security analysis, CBRN and counter-terrorism roles.
DMG 324/424, DMG 461, DMG 462, DMG 362; writing that stays calm and exact.
Media, communication and higher study
Reporting on disasters and climate; a master's (BRACU's MDM is in the same department).
DMG 497 in a media house, clear writing from every report, DMG 370 methods for a research master's.

facts: "Total Credits: 141 credits": General Education (GenEd) 36, Program Core Theory Courses 21, Program Core Lab Courses 12, Stream Specific Theory Courses 33, Stream Specific Lab Courses 15, Elective Theory Courses 12, Elective Lab Courses 3, Dissertation/ Capstone Project/ Study Abroad 6, Internship 3.

"Students will get a chance to choose one major stream from three streams according to their choices": Humanitarian Response (printed as "Option A: Humanitarian Assistance Design" in the course list), Climate Change Study (Option B) and Environmental Risk Reduction Technology (Option C); the pages do not say in which semester the stream is chosen.

DMG 497 Internship / Field Study (3 credits): "Students will be employed as an intern in any recognized organization for at least three months' time period" and "They will have to submit three items" - a portfolio, "A report of 8000 to 12000 words" explaining their achievements and learning in the working environment, and "A recommendation letter from the supervising personnel from the office".

Final requirement (6 credits), one of three: DMG 499 Dissertation - from a research proposal the student conducts the research, collects and analyses data and prepares "a dissertation document of 15000 to 20000 words under the supervision of a faculty member", then defends it "in front of an examiners' panel"; DMG 498 Capstone Project - "Based on a field study and survey" a report of 8000 to 12000 words under the supervision of a faculty member, presented "in front of an examiners' panel"; DMG 496 Study Abroad - one or more theory/lab/studio or field-study-based courses "in a recognized institute outside Bangladesh with the approval of the department chair or program head", "The course will be equivalent to 6 credits", with a minimum of 6 credits and GPA/CGPA equivalence "according to the university policy".
Detail of DMES page: "At the end all will complete an internship/field study and dissertation/capstone project/study abroad."

Fieldwork sits inside the lab courses: DMG 384 Damage & Need Assessment Lab covers "Fieldwork methods; Identification of hazards from field observations" with the learning outcome "Expert in conducting field work or field study"; DMG 112 is a geodetic surveying and mapping lab and DMG 383 a community vulnerability and capacity assessment lab.

Research methods are core: DMG 370 Qualitative Research Method (theory) and DMG 371 Quantitative Research Method and Statistical Data Analysis Lab I (lab), with DMG 471 Lab II offered as an elective lab.

"The program, approved by the University Grants Commission (UGC) of Bangladesh"; "Internships with various NGOs, government organizations, and media houses expose students" to the field; DMES provides student tutors for 100-level courses and runs DMES seminars and student events.

Admission test for Disaster Management: "English (Composition and MCQ)" only; minimum GPA 3.5 in SSC/equivalent and HSC/equivalent; candidates must pass each sub-section separately and are called for an interview for final selection.

Fees: BDM is not named on the Tuition and Fees page; it falls under "All other Program" - 8,250 per credit and semester fee 10,520 - plus "Admission Fee All Program 33,900" and the library membership fee of Tk. 2,500 (one time), for new students enrolled from Spring 2027.

Naming: the page calls the degree "Bachelor of Disaster Management" in most places and "B.A. in Disaster Management" in the structure section, and Program Highlights prints the majors as e.g. "Bachelor of Disaster Management in Environmental Risk Reduction Technology".

book.text: Read this first

This planner puts your whole DMES degree in one place: every published course, the rules that move your CGPA, the dates that cost money, and a working page for every week of the semester - on your phone, offline, with the arithmetic done for you.
What you are holding

items: **Degree** - the Bachelor of Disaster Management as BRACU prints it: every course, its credits and its prerequisite. Pick a semester and a grade per course and the CGPA, the credit map, the Ready / Locked checks and your semester-by-semester plan follow.
**CGPA** - the grading scale, a quick semester GPA, what it takes to reach a target, a retake what-if on BRACU's own rule, and the CGPA lines that decide waivers and standing.
**Money** - this semester's bill at the published rates, the whole degree roughly, and the dates that cost money with a countdown you can send to your calendar.
**Semester** - deadlines and tasks, your routine with a clash check, and the working pages of a semester (set-up, course pages, check-ins, finals plan), one set per semester.
**Toolkit** - the tools this department's work actually needs, with logs and calculators that count and flag as you type.
**Rules** - BRACU's own grading, retake, probation, load, scholarship and fee rules, with the source named under each.
**More** - clubs and careers, the printable pages, an assignment cover page, the Excel version of the tracker, and your backup.

book.text: What it is not

items: It is **not an official BRACU document**. Nobody at the university wrote, checked or approved it.
It does **not replace your advisor**, your advising sheet or the student portal. Those decide what counts toward your degree.

It is **a snapshot**. Course lists, fees, CGPA lines and dates were read from BRACU's own web pages on 20 October 2026. Universities change these. When a notice and this planner disagree - cross the old line out here, and the notice wins.

book.text: Start in 15 minutes

items: On **Home**, type your name, the semester you were admitted in and the semester you are in now.
On **Degree**, pick the semester and the grade of every course you have passed. Your CGPA appears at once, and every course shows Ready, Locked or Open.
On **Money**, type this semester's fee and drop dates from the Registrar's calendar; they count down on Home.
On **Semester**, put your sections into the routine and your deadlines into the task list.
Open the **Toolkit** when the work starts: labs, projects, cases, the final-year runway.

book.text: Your data

Everything you type stays in this browser on this device - nothing is sent anywhere, there is no account and no internet is needed. That also means a cleared browser or a new phone starts empty. So, now and then, open **More** and tap **Save this planner with my data inside**: you get this same file back with everything you have typed written into it. Keep that copy - open it on a laptop, send it to a new phone, or hand it to next semester's you.

If a browser refuses to keep your data between visits (some phones open files in a way that forgets), Home tells you so and offers the same button. Your planner is then simply the latest copy you saved.

Most students learn these rules by breaking one. Read them once now. Everything here is taken from BRAC University's published pages as they stood in October 2026; the source is named under each section.
The grading scale
BRAC University's undergraduate scale, in force since Fall 2020. Both A+ and A carry the full 4.0.
A+ to D- are passing grades. F is failing: it earns no credit and counts as zero in your GPA.
How your GPA and CGPA are worked out

Every course gives you **quality points = credits x grade point**. Add the quality points for a semester and divide by the credits you attempted for a letter grade: that is your semester GPA. Do the same across all semesters and you have your CGPA. The policy page prints the same formula: the sum of (grade points x credits) over the credits attempted.
Three things students get wrong

items: **An F stays in the sum until it is retaken.** It adds credits to the bottom of the fraction and nothing to the top.
**A D- passes, but it costs you.** A 3-credit D- is 2.1 quality points against 12.0 for an A - and a grade of B- or below is what the repeat rule exists for.
**W, I, P and AU never enter the GPA.** A W costs you the fee and the semester's work, not grade points.

Every student completes **DMG 497 Internship / Field Study (3 credits)**: at least three months as an intern in a recognised organisation, with three things to submit - a portfolio, **a report of 8,000 to 12,000 words** on achievements and learning in the working environment, and **a recommendation letter** from the supervising person at the office. Then one of three for the last **6 credits**: **DMG 499 Dissertation** (a research proposal, data collected and analysed, a dissertation of 15,000 to 20,000 words under a faculty supervisor, defended before an examiners' panel), **DMG 498 Capstone Project** (a field study and survey, a report of 8,000 to 12,000 words under a faculty supervisor, presented to an examiners' panel) or **DMG 496 Study Abroad** (one or more theory, lab, studio or field-study courses at a recognised institute outside Bangladesh, at least 6 credits, approved by the department chair or programme head, with the grade converted under university policy).
